claim: The pupillary light response is an important automatic physiological response which optimizes light reaching the retina.
source: The pupillary light response is an important automatic physiological response which optimizes light reaching the retina.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the pupillary light response.

claim: The pupil adjusts in response to illusory brightness and a range of cognitive functions.
source: Recent work has shown that the pupil also adjusts in response to illusory brightness and a range of cognitive functions
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to recent work in the field.

claim: The imagery pupillary light response correlates with objective measures of sensory imagery strength.
source: Here, we show that the imagery pupillary light response correlates with objective measures of sensory imagery strength.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The trial-by-trial phenomenological vividness of visual imagery is tracked by the imagery pupillary light response.
source: Further, the trial-by-trial phenomenological vividness of visual imagery is tracked by the imagery pupillary light response.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Individuals without visual imagery (aphantasia) do not show any significant evidence of an imagery pupillary light response.
source: We also demonstrated that a group of individuals without visual imagery (aphantasia) do not show any significant evidence of an imagery pupillary light response
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data comparing aphantasic individuals to controls.

claim: Aphantasic individuals show perceptual pupil light responses.
source: however they do show perceptual pupil light responses
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data on aphantasic participants.

claim: Aphantasic individuals show pupil dilation with larger cognitive load.
source: and pupil dilation with larger cognitive load
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data on aphantasic participants.

claim: The pupillary light response indexes the sensory strength of visual imagery.
source: Our results provide evidence that the pupillary light response indexes the sensory strength of visual imagery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: This work provides the first physiological validation of aphantasia.
source: This work also provides the first physiological validation of aphantasia.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the study's findings.

claim: Pupils constrict in response to brightness.
source: Pupils constrict in response to brightness whereas they dilate in response to dark conditions (known as the pupillary light response or reflex)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about pupillary responses.

claim: Pupils dilate in response to dark conditions.
source: Pupils constrict in response to brightness whereas they dilate in response to dark conditions (known as the pupillary light response or reflex)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about pupillary responses.

claim: Pupil constriction and dilation are driven by different neural pathways.
source: while these responses are related, they are considered to be driven by different neural pathways (see Mathôt, 2018 for a review)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Pupil responses were once thought to be driven only by afferent visual stimulation or automatic activation from emotional responses.
source: These involuntary pupil responses were once thought to be driven only by afferent visual stimulation, or automatic activation from emotional responses (Bradley et al., 2008; Partala and Surakka, 2003)
evidence: This is a historical claim about scientific understanding, supported by citations.

claim: Pupil size is sensitive to higher order perceptual and cognitive processes.
source: however, recent studies suggest that pupil size is sensitive to higher order perceptual and cognitive processes
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to recent studies.

claim: Greyscale images of the sun elicit greater pupil constriction than those of the moon.
source: For example, subjective interpretation of equiluminant stimuli, such as greyscale images of the sun elicit greater pupil constriction than those of the moon (Binda et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The target of covert visual attention can drive pupillary light responses.
source: The target of covert visual attention can drive pupillary light responses (Binda et al., 2013a)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Visual working memory content can drive pupillary light responses.
source: as can visual working memory content (Zokaei et al., 2019), but see Blom et al., 2016
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies, with a note about conflicting evidence.

claim: Mental imagery might be driving some cognitively induced pupil responses.
source: Further, evidence suggests that it might be mental imagery that is driving some of these cognitively induced pupil responses (Laeng and Sulutvedt, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents a hypothesis in the field.

claim: There are pupillary light responses when reading or listening to words conveying brightness.
source: and recent work has shown that there are pupillary light responses even when reading or listening to words conveying some level of brightness (Mathôt et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: It remains unknown if variations in pupil response to equiluminant stimuli are due to high-level semantic content or low-level visual imagery.
source: Hence, it remains unknown if the variations in pupil response to equiluminant stimuli are due to high-level semantic content or low-level visual imagery.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, identifying a gap.

claim: Visual imagery is considered a useful and often essential tool in many aspects of cognition.
source: Visual imagery is considered a useful and often essential tool in many aspects of cognition.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding about visual imagery.

claim: Visual imagery plays an important role in the retrieval of items from short- and long-term memory.
source: It plays an important role in the retrieval of items from short- and long-term memory (Pearson, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Visual imagery plays an important role in visual working memory.
source: visual working memory (Keogh and Pearson, 2011; Keogh and Pearson, 2014; Pearson and Keogh, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Visual imagery plays an important role in acquisition of language.
source: acquisition of language (Just et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Visual imagery plays an important role in spatial navigation.
source: and spatial navigation (Sack et al., 2005; Guariglia and Pizzamiglio, 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Visual imagery is used for simulating both past and potential future events.
source: It is also used for simulating both past and potential future events (Schacter et al., 2012; Schacter and Madore, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Visual imagery is used as a form of self-motivation for goal attainment.
source: the latter often as a form of self-motivation for goal attainment (Szpunar et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Large individual differences exist in visual imagery and its vividness.
source: As essential to cognition as it might appear, large individual differences exist in visual imagery and its vividness.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about visual imagery.

claim: Some people report imagery as so vivid it feels almost like perception.
source: Some people report imagery as so vivid it feels almost like perception
evidence: This is a description of individual differences in imagery experience.

claim: A small percentage of otherwise healthy people do not have the capacity for visual imagery at all.
source: while a small percentage of otherwise healthy people seemingly do not have the capacity for visual imagery at all – they report that when they think about how an object looks, there is no sensory-like experience of it whatsoever (Galton, 1880)
evidence: This claim is supported by a historical citation.

claim: The condition of lacking visual imagery has been recently termed 'aphantasia'.
source: This condition has been recently termed 'aphantasia' (Zeman et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the work that coined the term.

claim: Aphantasia can be congenital, persisting throughout one's lifetime.
source: it can be congenital, persisting throughout one's lifetime (Zeman et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Aphantasia can be acquired.
source: or acquired (Zeman et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Aphantasia is associated with a range of differences in general cognition.
source: is associated with a range of differences in general cognition (Dawes et al., 2020; Keogh et al., 2021a, Keogh and Pearson, 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Aphantasia is associated with dampened fear responses to imagined scary scenarios.
source: including dampened fear responses to imagined scary scenarios (Wicken et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The existence of aphantasia has been established using objective techniques that measure the low-level sensory elements of imagery.
source: The existence of aphantasia has also been established using objective techniques that measure the low-level sensory elements of imagery (Keogh and Pearson, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Participants who reported having visual imagery showed a clear pupillary light response to perceptual images.
source: Pupils showed a clear pupillary light response to perceptual images (Figure 1B; perception section; a significant effect of perceptual luminance F(1, 41) = 190.02, p < 0.001.)
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Imagery demonstrates a pupillary light response in the general population.
source: This trend was mirrored in the imagery period showing a significant main effect of imagery luminance (Figure 1B, box insets: imagery section; F(1, 41) = 67.42, p < 0.0001), indicating that imagery also demonstrates a pupillary light response.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: For Set-Size-One, pupil size in the Dark condition was significantly greater than in the Light condition during imagery.
source: Post hoc analysis using the Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons found that for both Set-Size-One and Set-Size-Four, the pupil size in the Dark condition was significantly greater than in the Light condition during imagery (p < 0.001 and p < 0.05, respectively, see Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by post hoc statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: For Set-Size-Four, pupil size in the Dark condition was significantly greater than in the Light condition during imagery.
source: Post hoc analysis using the Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons found that for both Set-Size-One and Set-Size-Four, the pupil size in the Dark condition was significantly greater than in the Light condition during imagery (p < 0.001 and p < 0.05, respectively, see Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by post hoc statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: There was no main effect of set size during perception.
source: There was no main effect of set size during perception F(1, 42) = 2.67, p = 0.11.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant main effect of set size during imagery.
source: However, there was a significant main effect of set size during imagery F(1, 41) = 6.48, p = 0.015, with less constriction/more dilation for Set-Size-Four (when averaged across the brightness conditions).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Pupil size is influenced by cognitive load.
source: This is consistent with previous studies suggesting that pupil size is influenced by cognitive load (Kahneman and Beatty, 1966; Laeng et al., 2011; van der Wel and van Steenbergen, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the Bright condition, Set-Size-Four resulted in significantly more pupil dilation during imagery than Set-Size-One.
source: Post hoc analysis also demonstrated that in the Bright condition, Set-Size-Four resulted in significantly more pupil dilation during imagery than Set-Size-One (p = 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by post hoc statistical analysis.

claim: In the Dark condition, pupil dilation during Set-Size-Four imagery was not significantly different to Set-Size-One.
source: However, in the Dark condition pupil dilation during Set-Size-Four imagery was not significantly different to Set-Size-One (p = 0.266).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Prior behavioural work suggests we have reasonable metacognition of visual imagery.
source: Prior behavioural work suggests we have reasonable metacognition of visual imagery, that is we are able to estimate the strength of imagery on a trial-by-trial basis (Pearson et al., 2011; Rademaker and Pearson, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There was a significant effect of vividness on pupil-difference scores.
source: A 2 × 4 linear mixed-effects analysis (2 (set size: 1, 4) × 4 (vividness rating: 1, 2, 3, 4)) demonstrated there was a significant effect of vividness (χ2(3) = 49.54, p = 1.004e−10), with larger pupillary light response for more vivid imagery trials (for both set sizes, see Figure 1D and fixed effects estimates in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The pupillary light response tracks the phenomenological vividness of visual imagery from moment to moment.
source: These data demonstrate that the pupillary light response tracks the phenomenological vividness of visual imagery from moment to moment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The binocular rivalry method allows the objective assessment of the sensory strength of imagery without relying on subjective reports.
source: To assess this, we utilized the binocular rivalry method (Pearson, 2014; Pearson et al., 2008), which allows the objective assessment of the sensory strength of imagery, without relying on any subjective reports (Chang and Pearson, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work describing the method.

claim: Within the general population, degree of pupil change in the Set-Size-One condition correlated positively with imagery strength measured using binocular rivalry.
source: Within the general population, degree of pupil change in the Set-Size-One condition correlated positively with imagery strength, using Pearson's correlation coefficient (rp(41) = 0.62, p = <0.0001, see Figure 2B: green circles and green trendline).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: A significant positive correlation was found between Set-Size-Four pupil-difference scores and binocular rivalry priming.
source: A significant positive correlation was found between Set-Size-Four pupil-difference scores and binocular rivalry priming (rs(41) = 0.46, p = 0.002, see Figure 2C: green circles and green trendline).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The sensory strength of imagery content is driving the imagery pupillary light response.
source: This provides further evidence that the sensory strength of imagery content is driving the imagery pupillary light response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between pupil response and binocular rivalry priming.

claim: Aphantasic participants showed a strong effect of stimulus luminance in the perceptual phase of the task.
source: Here, we again found a strong effect of stimulus luminance in the perceptual phase of the task for the aphantasic participants (Figure 3A: perception section; F(1, 17) = 81.18, p < 0.001), reflecting a functional pupillary light response.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Aphantasic participants showed no significant effect of luminance on pupil size during imagery.
source: However, we found no significant effect of luminance on pupil size during imagery Figure 3A, box insets: imagery section; F(1, 17) = 0.193, p = 0.67 and Figure 3B shows the lack of pupil diameter change for bright stimuli (red bars) and dark stimuli (blue bars).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: For aphantasic participants, there was no main effect of set size during perception.
source: Similarly, to the general population, there was no main effect of set size during perception F(1, 17) = 1.92, p = 0.18
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: For aphantasic participants, there was a significant main effect of set size during imagery.
source: however interestingly, there was a significant main effect of set size during imagery F(1, 17) = 6.185, p = 0.02, with greater pupil diameters for Set-Size-Four compared to Set-Size-One (when averaged across the brightness conditions).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Aphantasic participants were actively engaging in the imagery task and exerting greater cognitive effort for the larger set size.
source: This suggests that the aphantasic participants were actively engaging in the imagery task and exerting greater cognitive effort for the larger set size (van der Wel and van Steenbergen, 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the set size effect in aphantasic participants, supported by citation.

claim: 61.11% of aphantasic individuals had difference scores lower than or equal to 0 for set size one.
source: In comparison to the general population, 61.11% (11/18) of the aphantasic individuals had difference scores that were lower than or equal to 0 for set size one as compared to 9.5% (4/42) of the general population (see Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study, supported by data and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: 9.5% of the general population had difference scores lower than or equal to 0 for set size one.
source: In comparison to the general population, 61.11% (11/18) of the aphantasic individuals had difference scores that were lower than or equal to 0 for set size one as compared to 9.5% (4/42) of the general population (see Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study, supported by data and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Controls showed very strong evidence for a non-zero pupil-difference score.
source: Controls showed very strong evidence for H1 (BF10 > 1010; Bayesian one-sample t-test)
evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: The aphantasia population showed evidence for the null effect (no pupil-difference score).
source: whereas the aphantasia population showed evidence for the null effect (BF01 = 3.180)
evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: A direct comparison between control and aphantasia groups showed very strong evidence for an effect of group.
source: A direct comparison between the control and aphantasia groups using a Bayesian repeated measure analysis of variance (ANOVA; see Materials and methods) showed very strong evidence for an effect of group (BF10 > 106).
evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: Pupil-difference scores did not significantly predict imagery strength for the aphantasic population.
source: Finally, and as expected, pupil-difference scores (imagery of dark stimuli–bright stimuli) did not significantly predict imagery strength (measured using the binocular rivalry paradigm) for the aphantasic population (Figure 2B: yellow triangles; Set-Size-One: rp(17) = 0.20, p = 0.44); Set-Size-Four: (rp(17) = −0.08, p = 0.76).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Aphantasic individuals did not have any variation in their vividness ratings.
source: It should be noted that we could not perform an analysis on the vividness data in the same way as was done with the general population (Figure 1D) as the aphantasic individuals did not have any variation in their vividness ratings, reflecting their lack of subjective visual imagery (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sensitivity of the pupillary light response declines with age, beginning at 40–50 years old.
source: This factor is of particular importance because the sensitivity of the pupillary light response, as well as maximum pupillary constriction velocity and acceleration, are thought to decline with age, beginning at 40–50 years old (Fotiou et al., 2007; Lobato-Rincón et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Trial time-course pupil waveforms are very similar for both general and aphantasic populations.
source: However, trial time-course pupil waveforms are very similar for both general and aphantasic populations (Figures 1B and 3A, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by reference to Figures 1B and 3A.

claim: Both groups exhibited similar levels of pupil change during the perception phase of the task.
source: Both groups exhibited similar levels of pupil change during the perception phase of the task.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: There was a significant difference in pupil-difference score between general population and aphantasic groups when accounting for age.
source: Furthermore, a two-way ANCOVA was run on pupil-difference scores between general population and aphantasic groups with age as a covariate. Levene's test and normality checks were carried out and the assumptions were met. We found a significant difference in pupil-difference score (F(1, 57) = 4.763, p = 0.033) between the groups when accounting for age.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis controlling for age.

claim: Decreased pupil responsiveness with age was not driving the observed effects.
source: This provides evidence that decreased pupil responsiveness with age was not driving the observed effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ANCOVA analysis.

claim: There were no significant correlations between pupil diameter during perception and imagery for any condition.
source: We found there were no significant correlations between any of the perception and imagery conditions, or the difference scores for set size one and four (all p > 0.40, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Those individuals who have the largest pupillary light response while viewing images do not also have the greatest imagery driven pupillary light responses.
source: This lack of a correlation suggests that those individuals who have the largest pupillary light response while viewing the images, do not also have the greatest imagery driven pupillary light responses, making it unlikely that the pupil response while seeing the image is driving the mental imagery pupillary response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of correlation between perception and imagery pupil responses.

claim: There was no main effect of imagery group on pupil diameter during the perceptual period.
source: There was no main effect of imagery group F(1, 58) = 1.15, p = 0.29 and no significant interactions between imagery groups and any other factor (all p > 0.22, see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis, supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The observed pupil responses during the imagery period is unlikely to be a carry-over effect of the previous sensory response to perceived images.
source: These findings suggest the observed pupil responses during the imagery period of the task is unlikely to be a carry-over effect of the previous sensory response to perceived images.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of perceptual pupil responses.

claim: Pupil size depends on eye position.
source: Pupil size has been shown to depend on eye position (Drewes et al., 2014; Gagl et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pupil size depends on the preparation to make a saccade to an upcoming image.
source: and the preparation to make a saccade to an upcoming image (Jainta et al., 2011; Mathôt et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pupil modulation and eye position are controlled by largely overlapping circuitry.
source: Pupil modulation and eye position are also both controlled by largely overlapping circuitry (Wang and Munoz, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: There were no significant differences between the groups for the number of saccades made during perception or imagery of the stimuli.
source: There were no significant differences between the groups for the number of saccades made during perception or imagery of the stimuli (see Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by reference to supplementary figures.

claim: There were no differences in mean eccentricity values when comparing the two groups.
source: There were also no differences in mean eccentricity values when comparing the two groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: There was no correlation between eccentricity and the pupillary light response.
source: and no correlation with eccentricity and the pupillary light response (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: There was no correlation between eccentricity and binocular priming.
source: binocular priming (Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: There was no correlation between eccentricity and vividness ratings.
source: or vividness ratings (Figure 2—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Differences in fixation or eye movements between the two groups is unlikely to drive the observed group differences in the mental imagery pupillary light response.
source: suggesting that differences in fixation or eye movements between the two groups is unlikely to drive the observed group differences in regard to the mental imagery pupillary light response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of eye movements and fixation.

claim: It is the content and ability to form vivid visual images that is driving the imaginary pupillary light response.
source: Taken together these data from the general population and aphantasic individuals suggest that it is the content and ability to form vivid visual images, not the voluntary attempt to do so or the semantic content, that is driving the imaginary pupillary light response
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data from both populations.

claim: This work provides the first evidence that pupil changes are due to the sensory strength of imagery content and are not driven by higher-level semantic content.
source: providing the first evidence that these pupil changes are due to the sensory strength of imagery content and are not driven by higher-level semantic content.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claim: Our pupils respond to the vividness and strength of a visual image being held in mind.
source: Our results provide novel evidence that our pupils respond to the vividness and strength of a visual image being held in mind, the stronger and more vivid that image, the greater the pupillary light response.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The stronger and more vivid an image, the greater the pupillary light response.
source: Our results provide novel evidence that our pupils respond to the vividness and strength of a visual image being held in mind, the stronger and more vivid that image, the greater the pupillary light response.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: This work provides the first evidence linking the pupil response to strength and vividness of imagery within an individual as imagery vividness fluctuates from moment to moment.
source: Our data provide the first evidence linking the pupil response to strength and vividness of imagery, not only between individuals, but also within an individual as imagery vividness fluctuates from moment to moment (Dijkstra et al., 2017; Pearson et al., 2011; Rademaker and Pearson, 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, with citations to related work.

claim: As a group, there is no evidence of pupil response to imagery in individuals without mental imagery (aphantasia).
source: Finally, we show that, as a group, there is no evidence of this pupil response in individuals without mental imagery (aphantasia).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings for the aphantasic group.

claim: The imagery pupillary response may be a by-product of top-down modulation of midbrain-level visual circuitry.
source: One interpretation of these findings is that this imagery pupillary response is a by-product of the top-down modulation of midbrain-level visual circuitry (pretectal olivary nucleus, superior colliculus; Joshi and Gold, 2020), which occurs when imagining vividly, resulting in these regions interpreting this modulation as coming from external or afferent stimuli, and responding accordingly (Larsen and Waters, 2018; Schwalm and Rosales Jubal, 2017).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: The pupil would be responding to imagined luminance in much the same way that it responds to retina-based light sources.
source: In this case, the pupil would be responding to imagined luminance in much the same way that it responds to retina-based light sources.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Current data and models propose shared mechanisms between visual imagery and perception.
source: This is consistent with current data and models proposing shared mechanisms between visual imagery and perception (Dijkstra et al., 2017; Dijkstra et al., 2019; Ganis et al., 2004; Naselaris et al., 2015; Xie et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to current data and models.

claim: Visual imagery functions much like a weak version of afferent perception.
source: and the idea that visual imagery functions much like a weak version of afferent perception (Pearson, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The stronger or more vivid an individual's imagery is, the more 'perception like' their imagery is.
source: supporting the idea that the stronger or more vivid an individual's imagery is, the more 'perception like' their imagery is.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of existing theory.

claim: Pupil diameter might be encoded along with the original visual information and replayed during memory decoding to form the mental image.
source: An alternative mechanistic account might be that pupil diameter is encoded along with the original visual information for example bright object, and hence is replayed during memory decoding to form the mental image.
evidence: This is an alternative mechanistic speculation.

claim: Aphantasia has largely been defined using subjective means.
source: Aphantasia has largely been defined using subjective means (Dawes et al., 2020; Jacobs et al., 2018; Pounder et al., 2018; Zeman et al., 2015, but see Keogh and Pearson, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: People have remained sceptical about the true nature of aphantasia and its possible psychogenic basis.
source: Accordingly, people have remained sceptical about its true nature and possible psychogenic basis (de Vito and Bartolomeo, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Using a non-visual strategy to think about bright and dark objects does not induce a pupillary light response.
source: Our data demonstrate that using a non-visual strategy (no imagery in aphantasia) to think about bright and dark objects does not induce a pupillary light response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the aphantasia data.

claim: These data provide strong evidence linking the pupillary light response to mental imagery.
source: These data simultaneously provide strong evidence linking the pupillary light response to mental imagery
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data.

claim: These data support the behavioural work showing that aphantasic individuals lack visual sensory imagery.
source: as well as supporting the behavioural work showing that aphantasic individuals indeed lack visual sensory imagery (Keogh and Pearson, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and the current data.

claim: The pupillary light response is involuntary.
source: Because the pupillary light response is involuntary (Bouffard, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: These findings can be considered an unbiased neurophysiological measure of aphantasia.
source: we can consider these findings as an unbiased neurophysiological measure of aphantasia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the involuntary nature of the pupillary response.

claim: Pupillary light response can be an objective index of imagery strength in studies of imagery in general populations.
source: Not only do these data show that pupillary light response can be an objective index of imagery strength in studies of imagery in general populations
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the method.

claim: These data provide a new low-cost objective measure for aphantasia that is based on a physiological mechanism and not reliant on self-report.
source: our data also provide a new low-cost objective measure for aphantasia that is uniquely based on a physiological mechanism and not reliant on self-report.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the method for aphantasia research.

claim: Pupil size increased as a function of set size for aphantasic individuals when attempting imagery.
source: We think this is highly unlikely as pupil size did increase as a function of set size for aphantasic individuals when attempting imagery, as has previously been shown in the general population, demonstrating the typical relationship between cognitive effort or arousal and pupil dilation (Kahneman and Beatty, 1966; van der Wel and van Steenbergen, 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by citation to prior work on cognitive load.

claim: Aphantasic individuals were not simply 'refusing' to actively participate in the task.
source: This demonstrates active task engagement, suggesting that aphantasic individuals were not simply 'refusing' to actively participate in the task due to demand characteristics or a belief that they are unable to imagine (de Vito and Bartolomeo, 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the set size effect in aphantasic participants.

claim: There was no significant evidence of below chance performance for either group on either the binocular rivalry or pupillometry imagery tasks.
source: Further, we ran Bayesian one-sample t-tests on the binocular rivalry and pupillary light response difference scores (see Figure 2) comparing their performance to chance to see if there was any evidence they were performing significantly below chance. We found no significant evidence of below chance performance for either group on either the binocular rivalry or pupillometry imagery tasks (see Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a finding from Bayesian statistical analysis, supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: It seems unlikely that aphantasic individuals were not engaging in the tasks.
source: Taken together, with the set-size pupillary effect we observed in our aphantasic participants, it seems unlikely that our aphantasic individuals were not engaging in the tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: There was no significant evidence of an abnormal pupillary response in the aphantasic cohort when viewing images.
source: Further, there was no significant evidence of an abnormal pupillary response in our aphantasic cohort when viewing images
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The lack of an imaginary pupillary light response is likely due to aphantasic individuals' lack of visual imagery.
source: thus it is likely the lack of an imaginary pupillary light response is due to their lack of visual imagery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data.

claim: Aphantasic participants require greater cognitive effort to simultaneously maintain a larger number of shapes in their mind.
source: It also reveals that regardless of what imagery strategy aphantasic participants are implementing (e.g. propositional, spatial, language-like) to recall information about the shapes, they require greater cognitive effort to simultaneously maintain a larger number of shapes in their mind.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the set size effect in aphantasic participants.

claim: The study did not include catch trials in the pupillometry task.
source: One limitation of our study is we did not include catch trails in our pupillometry task, that is we did not include trials where we asked participants to report on what image they had been asked to imagine.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the study design.

claim: The study included catch trials in the binocular rivalry task through presenting mock binocular rivalry trials.
source: We did however include catch trials in our binocular rivalry task through presenting mock binocular rivalry trials.
evidence: This is a statement about the study design.

claim: If aphantasic participants are showing a response bias, we would expect to see a reduction in mock priming trials when compared to the control population.
source: If aphantasic participants are showing a response bias we would expect see a reduction in these mock priming trials when compared to the control population, which we did not find (see Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected if there were response bias, and a finding that this was not observed.

claim: Adding a simultaneous memory component to the task may lead some subjects to use a non-visual imagery strategy.
source: However, adding a simultaneous memory component to the task may lead some subjects to use a non-visual imagery strategy and as such, a reduction or dilution of the pupillary light response (see Pearson and Keogh, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential effects of adding catch trials, supported by citation.

claim: Future studies should include appropriate positive controls that allow for the identification of task engagement even when an individual doesn't have visual imagery.
source: Future studies of visual imagery, and even more importantly when investigating aphantasia, should aim to include appropriate positive controls that allow for the identification of task engagement even when an individual doesn't have visual imagery.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Perceptual pupillary light responses are not lingering throughout each trial and driving the observed imagery pupil response.
source: Another possible explanation of our results is that perceptual pupillary light responses are lingering throughout each trial and driving the observed imagery pupil response. If this is the case, then pupil responses during perceptual viewing and imagery should be correlated, however we did not find any such correlations (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of correlation between perception and imagery pupil responses.

claim: There is no significant difference in the perceptual pupillary responses between the general population and aphantasic individuals.
source: Further, when directly comparing the perceptual pupil responses between the general population and aphantasic individuals, there was no main effect of group or interaction between group and stimuli brightness or set size (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2). This demonstrates that there is no significant difference in the perceptual pupillary responses between the two groups
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis, supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: It is unlikely that aphantasic individuals' lack of an imagery pupillary response is due to a lack of perceptual response.
source: making it unlikely that aphantasic individual's lack of an imagery pupillary response is due to a lack of perceptual response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of perceptual responses.

claim: Participants who reported seeing after-images during the imagery period were excluded from the study.
source: Finally, we also asked participants if they perceived any after images during the imagery period and any participants who reported they did were excluded from the study.
evidence: This is a statement about the exclusion criteria used in the study.

claim: It is unlikely that the pupillary response to perceptually viewing the images is driving the observed imagery pupillary responses.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that it is unlikely that the pupillary response to perceptually viewing the images is driving our observed imagery pupillary responses, and the lack thereof in the aphantasic individuals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The pupillary light response during the visual imagery period reflects the wilful generation of imagery in the mind's eye of those who experience visual imagery.
source: Instead, it appears the pupillary light response during the visual imagery period reflects the wilful generation of imagery in the mind's eye of those who experience visual imagery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data.

claim: The strength of visual imagery correlates with the imagery pupillary light reflex but not the perceptual pupillary light reflex.
source: This is further substantiated by the strength of visual imagery (measured using the binocular rivalry paradigm) correlating with the imagery pupillary light reflex, but not the perceptual pupillary light reflex (see Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by reference to figures.

claim: Higher within-trial reports of vividness are reflected by greater pupillary light responses.
source: We also found that in the imagery task, higher within-trial reports of vividness are reflected by greater pupillary light responses (within-subjects effects; see Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Participants were able to accurately evaluate the vividness of individual episodes of imagery in comparison to other vividness episodes on previous trials.
source: This indicates that participants were able to accurately evaluate the vividness of individual episodes of imagery in comparison to other vividness episodes on previous trials.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the within-subjects vividness effects.

claim: Average vividness ratings did not correlate with pupil-difference scores.
source: However, average vividness ratings did not correlate with their pupil-difference scores, that is, participants who gave higher vividness ratings on average did not necessarily have increased pupil light responses in response to imagery (between-subjects effects; see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Participants' scores on the VVIQ did not correlate with pupil-difference scores.
source: Participant's scores on the VVIQ also did not correlate with pupil-difference scores (between-subjects effects; see Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Participants might have difficulties in accurately reporting their strength of sensory visual imagery on an absolute scale.
source: This suggests that participants might have difficulties in accurately reporting their strength of sensory visual imagery on an absolute scale (i.e. from 'no image' to 'as vivid as perception')
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of between-subjects correlations with subjective measures.

claim: The lack of between-subjects correlations brings into question the reliability of subjective measures of imagery.
source: and brings into question the reliability of these subjective measures of imagery and highlights the utility of using objective or online (i.e. in a task), and less trait-like measures when studying visual imagery.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the findings for imagery measurement.

claim: Pupil size is modulated by the content of visual working memory.
source: Recent studies have shown pupil size is also modulated by the content of visual working memory (Blom et al., 2016; Hustá et al., 2019; Zokaei et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Imagery has been implicated as one mnemonic that can be used to retain information in mind during visual working memory tasks.
source: It is interesting to note here that previous work has shown that imagery has been implicated as one mnemonic that can be used to retain information in mind during visual working memory tasks (Albers et al., 2013; Keogh and Pearson, 2011; Keogh and Pearson, 2014; Keogh and Pearson, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It is possible that imagery, being used as a mnemonic strategy, is driving the pupillary light response observed in visual working memory experiments.
source: This highlights the possibility that it is imagery, being used as a mnemonic strategy, that is driving the pupillary light response observed in visual working memory experiments (Pearson and Keogh, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying pupil responses in working memory tasks, supported by citation.

claim: Some participants report using a non-visual imagery strategy when remembering visual information.
source: Although many participants report using a visual imagery strategy during these tasks, some participants report using a non-visual imagery strategy when remembering visual information
evidence: This is a statement about individual differences in strategy use.

claim: Aphantasic individuals can perform traditional visual working memory tasks just as well as control populations.
source: and recent work demonstrates that aphantasic individuals can perform traditional visual working memory tasks just as well as control populations (Keogh et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: Measuring the pupillary light response in aphantasic individuals while performing visual working memory tasks may help elucidate differences in cognitive strategy use.
source: Measuring the pupillary light response in aphantasic individuals, and those who report not using an imagery strategy, while performing classic visual working memory tasks may help to further elucidate these differences in cognitive strategy use in a more objective manner.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The aphantasic sample contained a relatively small sample (18 participants) due to the relative rarity of this condition.
source: One limitation that is important to note here is that our aphantasic sample contained a relatively small sample (18 participants) due to the relative rarity of this condition.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the study.

claim: The two samples were not age matched.
source: Further our two samples were not age matched, which may have affected our results
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the study.

claim: Age differences are unlikely to be driving the findings because there was no difference between the two groups for the perceptual pupillary light response.
source: however seeing as there was no difference between the two groups for the perceptual pupillary light response, we think this is unlikely to be driving our findings.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of perceptual responses.

claim: Future studies should aim to replicate and extend these findings with a larger group of aphantasic individuals and age matched controls.
source: Future studies should aim to replicate and extend these findings with a larger group of aphantasic individuals and age matched controls.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: The pupillary light response can be used as a physiological index of individual differences in the sensory and phenomenological strength of visual imagery, including the lack of visual imagery – aphantasia.
source: To conclude, the present study demonstrates that the pupillary light response can be used as a physiological index of individual differences in the sensory and phenomenological strength of visual imagery, including the lack of visual imagery – aphantasia.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Combining the pupillary light response measure with the binocular rivalry paradigm will increase the reliability and objectivity of imagery test batteries.
source: Combining this measure with the binocular rivalry paradigm in favour of subjective alternatives will increase the reliability and objectivity of imagery test batteries and may lead to the development of more congenial theories of the mind's eye.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the findings for future research.

claim: Fifty-six psychology students with a mean age of 19.8 years were recruited for the study.
source: Fifty-six psychology students with a mean age of 19.8 years (range 18–31, 27 females) were recruited for the study and participated for course credit.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: The study aimed to obtain analysable data from a minimum of 40 participants.
source: We aimed to obtain analysable data from a minimum of 40 participants, which should be a large enough sample to identify a strong positive correlation between pupil dilation and imagery, which is what we would expect if imagery content were driving the previously observed imagery pupillary light response (g*Power effect size = 0.5, α = 0.05, β = 0.95).
evidence: This is a statement about the study design and power analysis.

claim: Fourteen participants were excluded from data analysis for not meeting a priori criteria, leaving 42 participants in the final general population sample.
source: Fourteen of these participants were excluded from data analysis for not meeting a priori criteria (see Exclusion criteria), leaving 42 participants in the final general population sample.
evidence: This is a description of the final sample after exclusions.

claim: Nineteen aphantasic individuals with a mean age of 35.8 years agreed to participate in the study.
source: We had nineteen aphantasic individuals agree to participate in the study with a mean age of 35.8 years (aged 18–54, 12 females).
evidence: This is a description of the aphantasic participants.

claim: One aphantasic individual was excluded from data analysis for not meeting a priori criteria, leaving 18 in the final sample.
source: One of these individuals was excluded from data analysis for not meeting a priori criteria (see Exclusion criteria), leaving 18 in the final sample.
evidence: This is a description of the final aphantasic sample after exclusions.

claim: Aphantasic participants had all contacted the lab regarding their aphantasia and asked to participate in the research.
source: These participants had all contacted the lab regarding their aphantasia and asked to participate in our research.
evidence: This is a description of how aphantasic participants were recruited.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected to normal vision.
source: All participants had normal or corrected to normal vision (i.e. glasses or contacts).
evidence: This is a description of participant inclusion criteria.

claim: Both experiments were approved by the UNSW Human Research Ethics Advisory Panel.
source: Both experiments were approved by the UNSW Human Research Ethics Advisory Panel (HREAP-C 3182).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.
